name: Krill oil

lead: Krill oil is an omega-3 supplement from Antarctic krill, with EPA and DHA carried on phospholipids and the carotenoid astaxanthin alongside. People take it for skin and general health, hoping less inflammation and a better skin barrier give calmer, healthier skin.

Several small trials report that it raises blood EPA and DHA about as well as fish oil, and the claimed advantage is better uptake. It is discussed for skin and inflammation, but no study has tested it for appearance. Fish oil has the larger outcome evidence base.

paras: It is taken as a daily softgel with a meal, usually as part of a general skin and health routine. Omega-3 changes build over weeks, and users often pair it with other skin-care habits.
Being crustacean-derived, it is not suited to shellfish-free diets. Krill research is newer and smaller than fish oil research, and harvest is regulated by CCAMLR.

angle.text: Krill oil is taken as a phospholipid-bound omega-3 source with astaxanthin: higher blood EPA and DHA are meant to lower inflammation and support the skin barrier, for calmer skin. It raises blood omega-3 in studies; skin effects are untested.

lead: Krill oil is a supplement extracted from Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba), a small crustacean. It supplies the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA largely bound to phospholipids, along with the carotenoid astaxanthin. [1]

It is compared mostly with fish oil, which carries the omega-3s mainly as triglycerides or ethyl esters. Several small trials report that krill oil raises blood EPA and DHA as effectively as or more than fish oil at lower stated doses, while fish oil has the larger evidence base for outcomes. [1][2][3][4]
It is listed under skin in the wiki because omega-3 supplements are discussed for skin and inflammation; no published trial located in the sources reviewed tests krill oil for appearance outcomes.

paras: EPA and DHA together form roughly 20-30% of krill lipid fatty acids, and krill harvesting is managed by the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, according to Grokipedia. [1] Commercial harvest began with Soviet expeditions in 1961-1962. [1]

A double-blind crossover study compared the incorporation of EPA and DHA into plasma phospholipids from krill oil and two fish-oil forms. [2] A trial in 113 people with normal or slightly raised cholesterol or triglycerides reported similar metabolic effects from krill and fish oil at a lower EPA and DHA content. [3] A four-week study reported a larger rise in the omega-3 index with krill oil than fish oil, and a study in overweight and obese adults reported higher plasma EPA and DHA after krill oil. [4][5] A mouse study found that DHA given as lysophosphatidylcholine, but not free DHA, increased brain DHA, and noted that standard fish and krill supplements do not. [6]

In rats, krill oil and fish oil matched for EPA and DHA differed in effects on ectopic fat and endocannabinoid-related inflammatory markers. [7] Reviews describe dietary omega-3 sources and fatty acid effects on hepatic steatosis. [8][9]

Bioavailability and lipid studies are summarised above. [2][3][4][5] Registered trials are testing krill oil for muscle protein metabolism, recovery after muscle-damaging exercise, sarcopenia, knee osteoarthritis pain, muscle weakness in type 2 diabetes and fasting triglycerides. [10][11][12][13][14] No studies found on skin appearance, wrinkles or acne.
